Share it with your friends! Facebook Twitter Google Pinterest Reddit Email LinkedIn Update: Unit 2 at the Cernavodă nuclear power plant will remain connected to the National Energy System after an overnight technical assessment found it can continue operating safely, state-owned Nuclearelectrica announced on Thursday, July 30. The decision followed concerns that both of the plant's reactors could be shut down because of historically low Danube water levels affecting the cooling system. "The operation of Units 1 and 2 of Cernavoda NPP is carried out based on strict monitoring of operating parameters and safety margins, as well as on procedures specific to drought conditions; thus, as long as the analysis of these parameters allows the operation in compliance with all nuclear safety norms, Unit 2 will remain connected to the National Energy System," reads the announcement. The company cautioned, however, that a shutdown of Unit 2 may still become necessary at any time, depending on changes in Danube water levels and their impact on the plant's systems. It said it will continue to monitor the situation and provide further updates. Initial story: Romania is to shut down both reactors at the Cernavodă nuclear power plant after the Danube's water level fell to exceptionally low levels due to severe drought, taking offline a facility that normally supplies around one-fifth of the country's electricity. Interim prime minister Ilie Bolojan urged households and large industrial consumers to reduce electricity use during evening peak hours as authorities prepare to rely more heavily on gas-fired generation and imports. State-owned nuclear power producer Nuclearelectrica announced on Wednesday, July 29, that it would carry out a controlled shutdown of Unit 2 after Unit 1 was taken offline earlier this week for the same reason. “Similar to the shutdown of Unit 1, Unit 2 will be shut down in a controlled manner due to the extremely low, unprecedented water level of the Danube caused by severe drought, in accordance with the plant’s procedures applicable in situations of severe drought," the company said in a filing to the Bucharest Stock Exchange. Nuclearelectrica explained that the decision follows the latest forecasts issued by the National Institute of Hydrology and Water Management (INHGA) and was taken in line with nuclear safety procedures. “Such measures are preventive and aim to protect nuclear safety and the reliability of the facilities," the company said, adding that it will reconnect the reactors once operating conditions allow. Speaking to Digi24 , prime minister Ilie Bolojan said the two reactors together produce about 1,300 MW, equivalent to nearly 20% of Romania's current electricity consumption. “We will be forced to start everything we can in terms of gas-fired generation, photovoltaic, storage and wind power and, at the same time, rely on imports," he said. The official described the period between 8:00 p.m. and 11:00 p.m. as the most critical for the electricity system and appealed to consumers to cut demand during those hours. “The critical period for electricity imports is in the evening, between 8:00 p.m. and 11:00 p.m. To give you an idea, out of Romania's current electricity demand of around 7,000 MW, we have been importing about 1,700 MW during those evening hours in recent days. This means we will have to import somewhat larger quantities. At the moment there are no problems with imports, but such problems could arise in the coming period," he warned. According to the prime minister, the effects of the drought are also being felt in other countries, including Hungary, where one of the units at the Paks nuclear power plant has been taken offline. According to current weather forecasts, the reactors could remain offline for one to two weeks if the drought persists. In an update on July 29, the National Administration Apele Române said the Danube's flow at the country's entrance is forecast to fall to around 1,500 cubic metres per second in early August, close to the record low of 1,400 cubic metres per second recorded in 1985. The current flow is about one-third of the long-term July average of 4,750 cubic metres per second. The water authority said severe drought conditions persist across the Danube basin and that no significant improvement is expected in the coming days, although there are currently no restrictions on public drinking water supplies. irina.marica@romania-insider.com (Photo source: Facebook/ Apele Române ) Read next 28 July 2026 Energy Low Danube water levels force shutdown of Cernavodă nuclear reactor in Romania Normal Energy Update: Romania keeps one nuclear power reactor online despite low Danube levels 30 July 2026 Irina Marica Like this article? https://www.politico.eu/article/meta-kid.text: BRUSSELS — The United States just made Meta change how it treats kids. The pressure's now on for Europe to prove its tougher tech laws can do the same — or go even further. Forty-seven U.S. states settled a landmark lawsuit with Meta for $18 billion on Wednesday, agreeing with the tech giant to set guardrails on its addictive design to better protect teenagers from harm. It is the culmination of a yearslong battle in one of the largest consumer protection settlements in U.S. history. From Brussels’ vantage point, it’s both a win for online safety and a loss of face for the European regulator, which has tried to get the social media giant to change its ways for years. Advertisement Advertisement The settlement on Wednesday details a series of changes that Meta needs to make to Facebook and Instagram over the next 10 years, including limiting daily time for minors on the platform, checking ages of users more rigorously and disabling cosmetic filters for teens. It has upped the ante for Brussels’ social media regulators. “Ironically, 9 measures out of 12 are covered by the [Digital Services Act], our law since 2023. U.S. courts are going faster than the EU Commission. We must ENFORCE DSA NOW!” former European Commissioner Thierry Breton, who negotiated and enforced the EU's social media rulebook up to 2024, wrote on X after the news of the settlement. German center-right lawmaker Andreas Schwab told POLITICO that Meta in the U.S. now "has even to go beyond what it offers to the European consumers.” Schwab, an architect of one of the EU’s Big Tech laws, the Digital Markets Act, called for Meta's policies in the two jurisdictions to be aligned. The European Commission in July accused Meta of breaching EU rules under the Digital Services Act by running addictive design features on Facebook and Instagram. In April, it accused Meta of breaking the same rules for not doing enough to keep under-13s off its platforms. The EU's investigation into addictive design and minors is more than two years old but has yet to yield concessions from the company or penalties for non-compliance. Spanish center-left European Parliament lawmaker Laura Ballarín Cereza asked the Commission on Thursday why Meta has committed to making changes only for U.S. users while it is in a discussion with EU authorities over the same issues. How will the Commission “ensure that EU citizens are not left with weaker protections than those in the US,” she wrote. Advertisement Advertisement Thomas Regnier, spokesperson for digital policy at the European Commission, said in a statement that it “is in continuous dialogue with Meta, who still has the possibility to offer commitments in the EU.” Meta has said it disagrees with the Commission's April and July findings. If it doesn't make changes to the EU's satisfaction, the firm risks facing a fine of up to 6 percent of its annual global revenue, which would amount to a maximum of $12 billion. Even if the full fine is imposed, which is highly unlikely, it's well under the $18 billion it settled for in the U.S. Europe wants more However, the changes Meta has pledged to make in the U.S. may not be as far-reaching as they seem — or meet the EU executive's demands. The Commission wants Meta to change, or at least offer users by default, a way out of the core addictive design features of its platforms — such as autoplay, infinite scroll and highly personalized feeds. The EU also demands remedies that limit time spent on the app and has previously dismissed Meta's time management and parental controls as not good enough. The settlement's proposed changes are "business as usual,” Jessica Galissaire, senior policy researcher at think tank Interface, told POLITICO about the EU's investigation. The Commission is asking for more far-reaching changes to the addictive design of the service, rather than just curtailing access to it, she said. “The platforms are starting to be scared of litigations," said Galissare. "It’s some steps in the in the right direction” but "we shouldn't settle for the lightweight changes that Meta is suggesting.” Advertisement Advertisement The settlement focuses on limiting access to the app at certain times as a default setting, and in many of these areas, teens or parents will be able to switch from these settings to less restrictive ones. Senior Commission officials have previously criticized Meta's parental controls for their complexity. But Meta will only give users the option to turn off the features most closely associated with engagement maximization, like autoplay and personalized feeds, instead of making them the default for every child, said Francesca Pisanu, senior policy officer at child rights group Eurochild. “The U.S. settlement establishes a combination of strong defaults, usage restrictions and parental controls, while the Commission’s preliminary approach more explicitly challenges the underlying engagement-maximising architecture of the platforms themselves,” said Pisanu. Leanda Barrington-Leach, executive director at the child rights group 5Rights Foundation, said: "Changes which focus on limiting children's access will not prevent continued exploitation and harm to children.” For now, Meta has held back from committing to roll out the changes it will make in the U.S. to users worldwide. It has said it will monitor how these changes are working in the U.S. and continue to engage with other governments. That's despite officials' explicit requests to do so in the U.K., South Korea and elsewhere. On Wednesday night, the U.K.’s Secretary of State for Work and Pensions, Pat McFadden, told Sky News he expected Meta to extend the changes to the U.K., saying the government didn’t want “a situation where young people in America have got a higher rate of protection than young people in the U.K.” Advertisement Advertisement

https://www.politico.eu/article/emmanuel.text: PARIS — French President Emmanuel Macron said on Thursday he told U.S. President Donald Trump that a 90-day diesel export ban being considered by the White House was a bad idea. “I think all the experts around him and all the American refiners can only tell him the same thing,” Macron said during a prime-time interview. “This decision would be a bad one — not just for the rest of the world, but for the U.S. economy as well.” The United States is currently the world’s largest exporter of diesel, according to ClearView Energy, and removing that supply from global markets would have far-reaching effects given how the conflict in the Middle East has already upended the global energy trade. Advertisement Advertisement “There is a war in the Middle East, and we are paying the price,” Macron said. The European Union has in recent months purchased more diesel from the U.S. to make up for lost supply that can’t get through the Strait of Hormuz, and shipments from across the Atlantic now make up more than half of all diesel imports to the bloc. Macron last week announced plans to chair a G7 meeting to look at releasing strategic oil stocks and held talks with the leaders of hydrocarbon exporters to secure supplies from alternative sources. During Thursday's interview, Macron said France would deploy the military to help secure the Saudi port city of Yanbu, from which more than 5 million barrels of oil are shipped daily, after it came under attack by the Tehran-backed Houthis in Yemen. The French leader has also tried to lobby Brussels to ease EU rules on the make-up of fuel and on methane emissions to help keep soaring energy prices under control, and his government this week announced it would spend €450 million to extend fuel subsidies enacted in March through the end of the year. But those moves have so far failed to move the needle, with diesel prices in France and the rest of Europe surging to record highs this week, according to analyses from Agence France-Presse. France has little fiscal space to further cushion the blow given its anemic growth, stubbornly high budget deficit and massive pile of debt. Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu said last week the government would propose a €54 billion budget squeeze to contain the deficit. Ben Munster and Geoffrey Smith contributed to this report . https://www.blisty.cz/art/136711-naza-th.text: NAZA or The Normalization of Atrocity: A film that cannot be unseen 12. 10. 2026 / Muriel Blaive I have just seen NAZA (2026), the documentary directed by Israeli filmmakers Yuval Abraham and Rachel Szor. The film premiered at the Venice Film Festival in September 2026, where it won the Special Jury Prize. It is an extraordinary work, one that performs an essential public service. It confronts us with realities that can no longer be ignored or denied. The film brings together the anonymous testimonies of 24 Israeli soldiers and intelligence officers involved in the surveillance, targeting, and bombing of Gaza. They describe how targets were selected, how algorithms were used, how civilian casualties were calculated and authorized, and how operations resulting in the deaths of entire families became routine. The title itself, NAZA , is an Israeli military acronym referring to collateral damage , a bureaucratic euphemism for the civilians expected to be killed during an attack on genuine terrorists. There is, of course, a particular historical difficulty in confronting atrocities committed by the state of Israel, founded in the aftermath of the Holocaust as a homeland for Jews, six million of whom had just been murdered. Our societies insist, quite rightly, on the singular horrors of the gas chambers and on the fact that the Holocaust was unprecedented in its industrialized extermination of European Jews. The difficulty arises when this experience of unparalleled victimhood fosters a sense of moral exceptionalism that can make it tempting to view atrocities committed by the Israeli state as fundamentally different from those once inflicted upon Jews. Historical exceptionalism can thus offer a misleading form of moral reassurance. Yet historical victimhood confers no exemption from moral responsibility. Whether the destruction of Gaza meets the legal definition of genocide is an important question, but it should not obscure the mass killing of civilians, the destruction of entire neighborhoods, and the immense scale of war crimes. Such atrocities require no comparison with the Holocaust to be condemned, nor does their moral gravity depend on whether they are ultimately classified as genocide. The dignity of victims is not a competition, and the recognition of one atrocity must never depend on the denial of another. You have to trust the system What is so chilling about NAZA is the form of mass murder it exposes: killing increasingly mediated by technology, algorithms, and the logic of a video game. Human beings become targets on a screen and responsibility dissolves into procedures. At one point, a participant describes having had doubts and turning to his supervisor, who tells him: "You have to trust the system." This soldier still hesitates, still questions, still has a conscience; but the answer is to stop questioning and trust the machinery. It would be tempting to blame artificial intelligence, but algorithms do not decide by themselves what human lives are worth. Someone designs and programs them, establishes the targeting criteria, and determines how many civilian casualties are considered acceptable. One of the witnesses describes a supervisor accepting a threshold of 15% civilian losses – that was subsequently exceeded anyway. These are human decisions, delegated to machines and then presented as if the machines themselves bore responsibility. As a historian familiar with the testimonies of soldiers during the Second World War, I found the parallels deeply unsettling. I kept thinking of Hannah Arendt's Eichmann in Jerusalem , in which she examines how Eichmann invoked orders and procedures to evade individual moral responsibility, and, more broadly, how ordinary people can participate in atrocities while convincing themselves that responsibility lies elsewhere. And then there is something singularly disturbing about Gaza: the enjoyment that one soldier now recalls with shame. When he first began directing drones to drop bombs, he recalls, it could feel like “zeh kef” (“it's fun”), almost like playing a video game. From the pursuit of terrorists to collective punishment A few days ago, I praised the Netflix series Fauda for its portrayal of the pursuit of terrorists responsible for the atrocities committed on October 7, 2023. The desire for revenge against the actual perpetrators who murdered one’s family or friends is perfectly understandable, even if one may question particular methods. But the distinction between targeting actual terrorists and targeting an entire population is fundamental. What NAZA documents is something altogether different. One witness describes a prevailing attitude: that no one in Gaza is innocent, not even children. Once such a degree of dehumanization is reached, there is virtually no limit to what can be justified – any massacre can be rationalized. Witnesses describe being instructed by their superiors to systematically destroy buildings, not because of any immediate military necessity, but precisely to ensure that the inhabitants would have nothing to return to. The destruction of homes and neighborhoods was, according to these testimonies, not an incidental consequence of warfare but a deliberate objective. Several witnesses also describe pressure to carry out as many bombings as possible while Israel still enjoyed sufficient international legitimacy, correctly anticipating that this legitimacy would gradually erode. International tolerance was thus treated as a temporary opportunity to intensify military operations before the political window closed. The silence of those who know What makes the film particularly chilling is the isolation of those who question what they have done. Only 24 people testify on screen, out of what must have been hundreds or thousands involved in these operations. They describe not only their own doubts, but the indifference of their colleagues, who do not share those doubts and do not want to hear them, and of Israeli society more broadly, which does not want to listen either. Of course, we cannot know how many others experienced such moral doubts or were troubled by what they witnessed. But the testimonies suggest a social environment in which questioning itself becomes unwelcome. One testimony particularly struck me. A soldier recalls visiting the Nazi concentration camps in Poland with his school class and being horrified by what the Germans had done. He subsequently became determined to join an elite military unit and worked hard to be accepted. I could not help thinking of Yoav Shamir's remarkable documentary Defamation (2009), which I have often cited in my own work. Shamir examined, among other things, Israeli school trips to the concentration camps in Poland and the way Holocaust memory was transmitted to young Israelis. His film exposed the dangers of the political instrumentalization of Holocaust memory, not by questioning the historical distinction between Nazi perpetrators and Jewish victims, which is beyond dispute, but by showing how that distinction can be projected onto contemporary conflicts. The problem arises when the historical experience of Jewish persecution is mobilized to portray Israel as the perpetual innocent victim and its adversaries as the successors of the Nazis, thereby discouraging critical reflection on the Israeli state's own actions and responsibilities. Some Israeli parents were already questioning these excursions, precisely because they feared their children were being subjected to emotional and ideological conditioning rather than historical education. Nearly twenty years later, the testimony in NAZA offers a chilling illustration of the attitudes against which Shamir was warning. The memory of historical victimhood, instead of fostering empathy for other victims, can become a source of moral certainty about one's own innocence and righteousness, even when participating in atrocities against others. The problem is not Holocaust remembrance itself, but what happens when remembrance becomes an instrument of collective identity rather than critical reflection. The film is also remarkably intelligent in its construction. It reminds us of Benjamin Netanyahu, decades ago, defining terrorism in terms of the indiscriminate killing of civilians. The irony of hearing that definition against the backdrop of what the film documents is devastating. There are echoes of Claude Lanzmann's Shoah (1985), and the extraordinary juxtaposition of Tel Aviv coming to a standstill for Yom HaShoah, the annual commemoration of the Holocaust, while the bombing of Gaza continues and a desperate father searches through the rubble for his children – the heartbreaking last scene of the film. The contrast is almost unbearable between a society capable of solemnly commemorating the victims of one historical catastrophe while remaining largely indifferent to the suffering inflicted in its own name. Throughout the film, there is also the contrast between the perfectly normal life continuing in Tel Aviv and the horror unfolding in Gaza. Again, as a historian of the Second World War, I found this unsettlingly familiar. Atrocities do not require the suspension of ordinary life; they can coexist with restaurants, cafés, family celebrations, commemorations, and the comforting conviction that one's own society is fundamentally decent. One atrocity does not cancel out another: escaping victimhood competition Yet it is absolutely crucial to hold two realities in mind at the same time. October 7 was a horrific massacre perpetrated by terrorists, whose crimes deserve punishment. The grief, outrage, and desire for justice of the victims' families are entirely legitimate. But can this justify the mass killing of civilians, especially of children, or the systematic destruction of Gaza? One atrocity does not cancel out another. Antisemitism is unacceptable, just as the dehumanization of Palestinians is unacceptable. There is no moral contradiction in condemning both Hamas's atrocities and the massive war crimes committed in retaliation by the Israeli military. On the contrary, the same moral principles demand both. As a historian, I cannot help thinking of the principle formulated by the German historian Bernd Faulenbach after reunification, when Germany had to confront the memory of both Nazi and Stalinist crimes. Faulenbach argued that Nazi crimes must not be relativized by reference to Stalinist crimes, and Stalinist crimes must not be minimized by reference to Nazi crimes. It was an attempt to escape victimhood competition – the temptation to use the suffering of one group to diminish or disqualify that of another. We desperately need the same principle today. There is no need to establish a hierarchy of suffering, to count the dead in order to determine whose suffering deserves recognition, or to engage in martyrological scorekeeping. The crimes must be investigated and judged on their own terms, but the dignity of the victims is never a matter of arithmetic. Every murdered civilian matters. Every child matters, whether Jewish or Palestinian. Human dignity is not conditional on belonging to the right people, or on having suffered more than someone else. What the film exposes is not simply the destruction of human lives, but the denial of the humanity of those whose lives are being destroyed. And this is precisely where the comparison with the Holocaust becomes meaningful without implying equivalence. The historical circumstances, the methods, and the scale may differ, but the mechanisms of dehumanization, the abdication of responsibility, the normalization of violence, and the willingness to exclude entire categories of human beings from the sphere of moral concern are disturbingly recognizable across different historical contexts. Recognizing these mechanisms is not relativizing the Holocaust; it is taking seriously what the study of that history can teach us. Impossible to unsee As a Czech viewer described it yesterday in a testimony published in Britské listy , when NAZA ended, the audience remained sitting in shocked horror. I experienced exactly the same reaction today: when the film ended, nobody moved or spoke. Part of what makes the film so devastating is that it leaves so little room for the comforting explanations through which we ordinarily distance ourselves from atrocities. These are not incomprehensible monsters acting outside history; they are ordinary human beings, operating within institutions, obeying instructions, trusting procedures, sometimes questioning, sometimes enjoying what they do, and living in a society that largely prefers not to know. I feel immense admiration and gratitude for the courage of those who agreed to testify, despite the personal and social consequences they may face, and for the filmmakers who brought their testimonies to light. NAZA is an excellent film. Devastating, indispensable, and impossible to unsee. Diskuse Související články Channel 4 News: NAZA: Film, který šokoval izraelskou společnost. https://www.politico.eu/article/eu-offer.text: European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen announced Monday that the EU will help finance some Black Sea security costs after attacks on commercial shipping — blamed on Russia — even as the main diplomatic push to end the crisis unfolds elsewhere. "Threats, attacks and incursions are rising off the coasts of the Black Sea," von der Leyen said at the start of her visit to Romania. In response, she said the bloc will “fast track the work on the Black Sea Maritime Security Hub, with a clear timeline for completion and dedicated funding of €50 million.” Advertisement Advertisement She also announced an additional €10 million in EU cash for Romania’s search-and-rescue operations. The sums are tiny compared to the €16.7 billion Romania is getting under the EU's SAFE arms loans program . The hub, announced last year, is a joint control center to be run by Romania and Bulgaria and is expected to be fully operational by the end of the year. It aims to monitor maritime activity in real time and safeguard vital infrastructure such as undersea power and communication cables. It would offer both countries a unified view of the sea and sky, helping them detect threats before they strike. Monday's announcement follows weeks of mounting violence on the Black Sea. Since early October, at least nine ships have been struck in the exclusive economic zones of NATO and EU members Romania and Bulgaria; four were sunk, and 34 sailors are dead or missing. Other ships have been hit off Russia's shores. Both Romania and Bulgaria raised the issue at last month's meeting of EU leaders and are pressing for more security support. However, while Romania has blamed Russia, Bulgaria has stopped short. Von der Leyen is set to visit Varna, on Bulgaria’s coast, on Tuesday. Advertisement Advertisement Meanwhile, the U.S. is steering talks on a Black Sea ceasefire and an agreement on safe passage, with Secretary of State Marco Rubio saying Washington is reviewing proposals from Turkey forwarded in late October and is “open” to ideas from India. An agreement would not end the conflict, Rubio said, but it would “solve a unique aspect” of it by easing the spillover on food security for vulnerable nations. EU foreign policy chief Kaja Kallas said on Oct. 21 that the bloc is working with Turkey, India and food-importing countries in Africa and other regions on a freedom-of-navigation deal. Ukraine has agreed to such an arrangement, she added, but Russia has rejected it. A shipping container lies stranded on rocks near Arapya, Bulgaria on Nov. 3, 2026. | Hristo Rusev/Getty Images Von der Leyen said the EU backs Ukraine’s call for a Black Sea ceasefire, referring to “the peace talks taking place in Abu Dhabi tomorrow with European presence.” Commission chief spokesperson Paula Pinho gave no details on the proposals or the EU’s role. She noted a “common interest” in resolving disruptions, but declined to comment on the intentions of Turkey or the U.S. Asked whether he foresaw a possible breakthrough this week, Ukraine’s Agriculture Minister Taras Vysotskyi was pessimistic. He said that Kyiv is “preparing to keep our farmers operating without access to the deep-water Black Sea ports for the long term.” Advertisement Advertisement The Black Sea matters to both sides in the war. The ports of Ukraine's Greater Odesa region are main channels for its exports, including steel, iron ore and grain, and they bring in billions of dollars. Several ships hit in EU waters were carrying Ukrainian grain. Most of Russia’s grain exports also leave through Black Sea ports such as Novorossiysk, a major oil export hub, along with Tuapse. Other countries are deeply invested, too. Near Novorossiysk, the Caspian Pipeline Consortium terminal, partly owned by U.S. oil giants Chevron and Exxon, handles about 80% of Kazakhstan’s crude exports. Turkey has suffered the most ship attacks, and tankers headed for Georgia have also come under fire. Agnes Rønberg contributed reporting. Advertisement Advertisement
